title: Whole-world versus isolated-branch generation and merge
question: For a binary ethical choice, does generating each action graph independently and then merging outperform generation of the complete comparative world?
hypothesis: Branch isolation will reduce graph-construction complexity and repair burden while preserving enough source context for a valid deterministic merge.

change_under_test.description: Compare one two-action graph-generation route with two independent one-action routes followed by deterministic merge.

control.description: Generate both oxygen-allocation action branches in one world model.

experimental.description: Generate the Eli and Noor action graphs independently, then merge only if both commit.

intentionally_not_compared: cross-action counterfactual completion after a successful merge
interpretation: On this case, the complete-world route correctly represented both allocation branches. Isolated generation repeatedly made the nonrecipient state DIRECT and lost valid action-mediated ancestry. The comparative world supplied useful exclusivity and ownership context rather than merely adding complexity.

keep: binary branch merger as an experimental utility
branchwise runner for additional controlled comparisons
do_not_prioritize: replacing whole-world generation with isolated one-action generation
putting branchwise generation on the default execution path
decision.next_test: If revisited, supply each isolated branch with an explicit branch contract containing actor, recipient, nonrecipient, exclusivity, and source-clause ownership, then test on a frozen multi-case set.

limitations: This is one stochastic live scenario and does not establish general superiority.
The branches saw the full source scenario but only one canonical action, which changes action-coverage expectations as well as generation scope.
The merge could not be evaluated because neither isolated branch committed.
An earlier attempted run was invalid because all model calls failed at the network boundary and is excluded from the comparison.
Wall-clock time includes variable remote-model latency.
